title: Three warnings on AI in finance arrive in one week
dek: A Fed governor, the IMF and the analytics arm of a Thai bank each warn about a different strain from AI.

body.head: Agents at the customer account
body.text: Federal Reserve Governor Michael Barr told a conference in Milan that major banks now report finding AI agents attempting to take actions in retail customer accounts, without the bank being able to verify authenticity, consent, and alignment with customer instructions. Banks, and the teams who run their fraud and operations desks, now have to ask who is really acting on an account.
support: For example, major banks now report finding AI agents attempting to take actions in retail customer accounts, without the bank being able to verify authenticity, consent, and alignment with customer instructions.
At the Seventh Annual Association for Computing Machinery International Conference on Artificial Intelligence in Finance, Milan, Italy

body.head: Runs at machine speed
body.text: Barr also said AI agents may accelerate deposit outflows during stress periods, potentially accelerating runs that unfold in minutes and overwhelming traditional liquidity management and regulatory intervention timelines. His guardrails are strict authentication, explicit consent verification for specific actions and technical controls limiting agent capabilities, which is a checklist a bank can start from today.
support: In addition, AI agents may accelerate deposit outflows during stress periods.

Where customers once needed to execute transfers, AI agents could instantaneously detect yield differentials or stability signals and autonomously move funds at high speed, potentially accelerating runs that unfold in minutes, overwhelming traditional liquidity management and regulatory intervention timelines.

These incidents underscore that AI in financial services can only succeed long term with appropriate guardrails: strict authentication, explicit consent verification for specific actions, technical controls limiting agent capabilities, and both rules- and values-based constraints.

body.head: The IMF looks at the money behind AI
body.text: IMF Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva said the global economy is "on the AI leg" and warned that overdependence on the sector risks the world's financial stability. The IMF estimates circular financing among AI companies at a little over $1 trillion, two-thirds of it funded by debt, while Georgieva called the recent market swings "orderly".
support: The global economy is "on the AI leg," International Monetary Fund Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva said Monday, warning that the overdependence on the sector risks the world's financial stability.

Circular financing among AI companies — where money invested in an AI company ultimately flows back to the investor through purchase orders — has grown to a little over $1 trillion, two-thirds of it funded by debt, the IMF estimates.
Georgieva on Monday characterized the recent market swings as "orderly," and unlikely to spiral into anything that could undermine the world economy, while urging caution.

body.head: Thailand shows the exposure
body.text: In Thailand, ttb analytics said on November 9 that growth in Thailand is heavily concentrated in AI-linked electronics, and that if the global AI boom has a bubble burst, the impact on Thailand will be immediate and pronounced, especially within financial markets. Its baseline 2026 growth projection moved from 2.4 percent to 2.7 percent.
support: Growth is heavily concentrated in AI-linked electronics.

If the global AI boom experiences a bubble burst, the impact on Thailand will be immediate and pronounced—especially within financial markets—because we are formally indexed as a key upstream and downstream supplier.

By resolving long-standing discrepancies between booming export values and previously contracting manufacturing indicators, the MPI rebasing automatically upgraded Thailand's baseline GDP growth projection from 2.4 percent to 2.7 percent for 2026.

Speaking at a media briefing on Monday, 9 November 2026, Dr Naris Sathapholdeja , head of TMB Data and ttb analytics at TMBThanachart Bank (ttb), presented an upgraded economic outlook while calling for urgent structural reforms to ensure sustainable growth.

body.head: Two questions for this week
body.text: Put side by side, one warning is about how fast and how safely software can act inside a bank, and the other two are about how much of the economy and its financing now sits on AI. For our own desks, we can ask which accounts and approvals an agent could touch, and which of our exposures lean on the same AI-linked growth.

suggestion: A line on which of your own clients' exposures lean on AI-linked growth would fit in the last section.
